opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic story is something like this. For a while, a lot of the progress we were seeing came from scaling pretraining: bigger models, more data, more compute. There was a real question about how far that would go. You eventually run into data constraints, and the returns from each additional order of magnitude of pretraining compute seemed to be getting more expensive to realize in terms of capabilities people actually care about.

Then reasoning models came along, where you take a pretrained model and do reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes: math problems, coding problems, things where you can check whether the answer is right. What was striking is that this seemed to work quite well, and early on it was being done with a pretty small amount of compute relative to pretraining. So you have this new axis of scaling where you're nowhere near the limits yet. You can potentially scale RL compute by several orders of magnitude before it's comparable to what's spent on pretraining.

Why does that matter for timelines? A few reasons.

First, it means the "we're going to hit a wall soon" story looks weaker. Even if pretraining returns diminish, there's another lever that seems to give substantial gains, and labs can pull it fairly quickly because the infrastructure already exists.

Second, the kinds of capabilities RL improves are close to the ones that matter most for automating AI research and software engineering. RL is training models to do long chains of reasoning, to try things, check their work, recover from mistakes, and increasingly to act agentically over longer horizons. That's much closer to "can this thing do the job of a research engineer" than "can it predict the next token well."

Third, there's a question of how general the gains are. If RL only made models better at narrow, easily checked tasks, that would matter less. But my sense is there's meaningful transfer, and even if not, coding and math are exactly the domains you most need for an AI R&D feedback loop. If you can automate a large fraction of AI research engineering, things could speed up a lot from there.

I want to be careful not to overstate it. There are real uncertainties. We don't know how well RL scales to really long-horizon tasks where feedback is sparse or hard to verify. We don't know how much of the early gains were low-hanging fruit. And there's a question of whether you can build enough good RL environments at scale. So I don't think this settles anything.

But overall I updated toward somewhat shorter timelines. Before, my view had more weight on scenarios where progress stalls for a while after pretraining saturates. Now there's an obvious next thing to scale, it's producing gains on exactly the capabilities that matter for transformative AI, and there's a lot of room left. That pushes me to put more probability on very capable systems, the kind that could substantially automate AI R&D, arriving within something like the next five to ten years, with meaningful probability on the earlier end of that.

r001.rationale: The response mentions long chains of reasoning and increasingly agentic, longer-horizon behavior, but does not clearly identify extending RL from narrow, single-step tasks to multistep agentic tasks as a substantial untapped source of gains.

r002.rationale: It discusses scaling RL compute and separately notes uncertainty about building enough RL environments, but does not distinguish environment diversity as a separate scaling dimension.

r003.rationale: It says RL compute could scale by several orders of magnitude before matching pretraining compute, but gives no claim that this could happen within the next year.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand is that before the reasoning model paradigm, the way we got better models was basically pretraining scale-up, and that was getting expensive. Each generation was something like a 10x increase in compute, and the gains per order of magnitude were real but kind of modest. And you could look at that and say, "Okay, we're going to run out of data, we're going to run into cost constraints, and so maybe progress slows down."

What happened with RL on reasoning models — o1, o3, DeepSeek R1, that whole line — is that it opened up a second axis of scaling that was, at least at the start, extremely cheap. The amount of compute that went into the RL phase of these early reasoning models was tiny relative to pretraining. We're talking maybe a percent or a few percent of the total compute, and yet it produced these enormous gains on math, on coding, on anything with a verifiable answer. So you have this situation where there's a huge overhang: you've found a technique that works, and you've barely scaled it at all.

And the reason that's important evidence for timelines is that we have a pretty good track record of what happens when you take something that works at small scale and pour orders of magnitude more compute into it. It usually keeps working for a while. So my expectation was, and I think it's largely been borne out, that labs would take RL compute from a few percent of the budget up to comparable to pretraining, which is a 10x, 100x, maybe more increase in that specific input. That's a lot of additional "free" progress that you get just from scaling, without needing any new ideas.

The other piece is what RL is actually buying you. It's not just raw capability on benchmarks. It's things like the ability to work on a task for a long time without going off the rails, to check your own work, to recover from errors. Those are exactly the properties you need for models to do long-horizon autonomous work, which is the thing that actually matters for AI accelerating AI research. So when I see that the length of tasks models can do roughly reliably has been doubling every several months, and that a lot of that is coming from the RL side, that updates me toward thinking the path to something like automated AI R&D is shorter than I would have guessed a couple years ago.

Now, I want to be careful here. There are reasons to think it might not keep going. RL on verifiable tasks is easiest where you have a clean reward signal, and a lot of economically useful work doesn't look like that. The gains could saturate. There's a question of whether you get transfer from math and code to messier domains. And the fact that it was cheap at first means some of the easy wins have already been taken, so the next 10x might buy you less than the last 10x did. I don't think RL scaling alone gets you to full automation of AI research.

But the overall picture is: we had one scaling lever that was getting expensive, and then we found a second one that was cheap and very effective, and there was a ton of room to push it. That's the kind of thing that should make you take shorter timelines more seriously. It doesn't make me confident we'll get there by 2028 or whatever, but it moved my median noticeably, and I think it should move most people's.

astra-6.text:
The basic reason is that it gives us another way to turn more compute into more capability. Previously, a lot of the evidence for progress came from pretraining: you train on more text with a bigger model, and performance gets better. But there were questions about how far that could go, particularly as you run out of high-quality human-generated data.

With reinforcement learning for reasoning, you can have the model attempt a problem, check whether it got the right answer, and train it to produce successful solutions more often. In domains like maths and programming, you can do some of that checking automatically. So you potentially have a way to keep improving without needing humans to write out every example of good reasoning.

The important evidence isn’t just that reinforcement learning helps. We already knew that it could help. It’s that spending substantially more compute on it appears to produce substantial improvements in capabilities that matter. That makes it more plausible that companies can take the enormous compute budgets they’re planning and use them productively over the next few years.

There’s also a connection to automating AI research. If these methods make models much better at programming and solving technical problems, that could help automate the work of developing better AI systems. You don’t need the model to become equally good at every human activity for that to have a big effect on timelines.

I wouldn’t treat this as proof that the approach scales all the way to systems that can automate AI research. It could plateau, and progress on problems with easily checked answers might transfer imperfectly to messy research tasks. But it shifts probability toward shorter timelines because one of the things we were uncertain about—whether there was another scalable source of substantial capability gains—now looks more plausible.

r003.rationale: It says substantially more compute and large budgets could be used over the next few years, but gives no claim of scaling RL compute by more than two orders of magnitude within the next year.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic reason is that it gives us another way to turn more compute into more capable models. Previously, a lot of the case for continued progress was about scaling pretraining: train bigger models on more data. And there were questions about how much useful data you could get and how far that approach would take you.

With reinforcement learning, you can instead have the model attempt problems, check whether its answers are right, and train it to produce the kinds of reasoning that lead to correct answers. If that scales well, then even with the same underlying pretrained model, spending substantially more compute on this process could produce substantially better capabilities.

You also get the ability to spend more compute at inference time—to let the model think longer on a particular problem. Those are related, because training can teach the model to use that additional thinking effectively.

The important uncertainty is how far this generalizes. Getting better at math or programming problems with easily checked answers doesn't automatically mean getting better at every aspect of research. But math and programming are themselves pretty relevant to AI research. So if this approach keeps working, it makes a world where AI systems can substantially accelerate further AI development more plausible, sooner. That's why I see it as meaningful evidence for shorter timelines, even though it doesn't by itself establish a particular date.

r001.rationale: The response discusses RL on problems with checkable answers and longer inference-time thinking, but does not identify expanding from narrow, single-step tasks to multistep agentic tasks as an untapped source of gains.

r002.rationale: It discusses spending more compute on RL, but does not distinguish that from increasing the diversity of RL environments.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate that RL compute could increase by more than two orders of magnitude within a year.
